title: Thirty parts
hookLine: divided into thirty parts so it can be read in a month

lines: THE WHOLE BOOK IN A MONTH.
cards: In Ramadan, in mosques all over the world, something happens night after night. After the evening prayer comes the long night prayer, tarawih, and the imam recites from the Qur'an.
In some mosques it's a set amount each night, so by the end of the month the whole book has been heard, cover to cover. But the book has one hundred and fourteen surahs of wildly different lengths.
How do you split it into equal nights?

teach.b: The Qur'an is divided into thirty parts of roughly equal length. Each is called a juz', which simply means a part, a portion. One juz' a day takes you through the whole book in a month.
Each juz' splits into two halves, each a hizb, sixty in all, and those into quarters. Open a mushaf and you'll see the markers in the margins.
Here's the thing to know: these divisions aren't part of the revelation, and tradition doesn't trace them to the Prophet ﷺ.

They were added later, as a reader's aid, by measuring length, not following meaning. So a juz' can begin in the middle of a surah, even in the middle of a story. The second starts partway through al-Baqarah.
Many are known by the words they begin with. And the thirtieth is the one you know.

It's usually called Juz' 'Amma, after its first word, 'amma, about what, from the opening of An-Naba': about what are they asking one another? That's the part you walked through in camp four, from An-Naba' to An-Nas.
The Prophet advised a companion, Abdullah ibn Amr, to finish the Qur'an in a month. When Abdullah said he could do more, he was told: then in seven days, and not less.
From that, some Muslims divide the book into seven portions, one for each day of the week. The thirty parts are the rhythm printed in the margins.

how: Reading one juz' a day in Ramadan is a common practice, and some mosques recite one juz' a night in the tarawih prayer so the whole Qur'an is heard by the end of the month.

games.q: you're Abdullah ibn Amr. the Prophet tells you to finish the Qur'an in a month. you say you can do more. what's his answer?
o: then in seven days, and not less.
games.why: seven days, and not less. the month and the week both became rhythms Muslims still read by.

practice: Count on your fingers the parts you already know: al-Fatiha is in the first juz', Ayat al-Kursi, if you know it, in the third, and the short surahs from camp four in the thirtieth.
If you pray, recite one short surah from the thirtieth juz' now, slowly; if you're learning, just say its name and remember the day you met it.

wordCard.voice: Juz'. A part: one of thirty equal portions of the Qur'an, so the whole can be read in a month. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: a part, a portion. plural: ajza'. the final sound is a short catch in the throat.

carryVoice: Your line: thirty parts, thirty nights. A whole book, one portion at a time. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 5054 (Abdullah ibn Amr: finish it in a month; then in seven days, and not less)
